questions.question: What is a healthy Git workflow for a team?
questions.title: A Healthy Git Workflow
questions.direct_answer: A team workflow: 1) main is always deployable; 2) create a feature branch per task (git switch -c add-login); 3) make small, focused commits with clear messages (git commit -m 'add login form'); 4) push the branch (git push -u origin add-login); 5) open a pull request for review; 6) address review comments; 7) merge to main (or squash) after approval; 8) pull main regularly (git pull) to stay current. The rules: never commit directly to main, write messages in the imperative ('add' not 'added'), keep branches short-lived, and rebase or merge to incorporate main's changes. Small, reviewable PRs beat huge ones.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you describe branch-per-feature, small commits, PR review, and 'main is always deployable', and know the commands.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Committing straight to main, or huge long-lived branches that become hard to merge.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Branch per feature, small focused commits, PR for review, merge to main after approval. main is always deployable; never commit straight to main.

sections.title: What the interviewer wants
sections.content: Define A Healthy Git Workflow simply, show a small example, and mention the main trade-off or edge case.

sections.title: Branch, Commit, Review, Merge
sections.content: A team workflow: one, main is always deployable. Two, create a feature branch per task with git switch -c add-login. Three, make small, focused commits with clear messages — git commit -m add login form. Four, push the branch with git push -u origin add-login. Five, open a pull request for review. Six, address review comments. Seven, merge to main, or squash, after approval. Eight, pull main regularly with git pull to stay current. The rules: never commit directly to main, write messages in the imperative (add, not added), keep branches short-lived, and rebase or merge to incorporate main's changes. Small, reviewable PRs beat huge ones that no one can review well.

sections.title: The Team Loop
sections.content:
main deployable -> branch -> commit -> PR -> review -> merge.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  M[main: deployable] --> B[branch: add-login]
  B --> C[small commits]
  C --> P[push + PR]
  P --> R[review]
  R --> Me[merge to main]
```

sections.title: A team workflow
sections.content:
```ruby
# 1) main is always deployable; branch per task
git switch -c add-login

# 2) Small, focused commits (imperative messages)
git add app/controllers/sessions_controller.rb
git commit -m 'add login form and session creation'
#   (NOT: 'added some stuff' or 'wip')

# 3) Push the branch
git push -u origin add-login

# 4) Open a pull request -> review -> address comments

# 5) Merge to main after approval (or squash for a clean history)
git switch main
git pull                    # stay current
git merge add-login
git push

# Rules: never commit to main; short-lived branches; pull main often.
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Committing straight to main — no review, hard to revert, breaks deployability.
Huge long-lived branches — they drift and become hard to merge.
Vague messages ('wip', 'fix') — the history is unreadable later.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: A healthy workflow: main is always deployable; branch per feature.
Make small, focused commits with imperative messages ('add', not 'added').
Push the branch and open a pull request for review; address comments.
Merge to main after approval; pull main regularly to stay current.
Never commit straight to main; keep branches short-lived and reviewable.

sections.title: Spoken Answer

Three, make small, focused commits with clear messages — git commit -m add login form. Four, push the branch with git push -u origin add-login. Five, open a pull request for review. Six, address review comments. Seven, merge to main, or squash, after approval. Eight, pull main regularly with git pull to stay current. The rules: never commit directly to main, write messages in the imperative (add, not added), keep branches short-lived, and rebase or merge to incorporate main's changes. Small, reviewable PRs beat huge ones that no one can review well. A common mistake is committing straight to main, with no review and hard to revert, and huge long-lived branches that drift.
